To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in two patients with PH1, the AGT enzyme was rerouted from the peroxisome to the mitochondria, resulting in a more severe clinical phenotype.

in two patients with PH1, the AGT enzyme activity and immunoprecipitated protein were largely mitochondrial, not peroxisome, and these two individuals were more severely afflicted with the disease than expected from the level of their residual AGTs activity.
two patients with primary Hyperoxaluria type I have a defect in the normal trafficking of the enzyme alanine/glycolate aminotranferase from peroxisomes to mitochondria.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular basis of the disease known as Primary Hyperoxaluria Type I.
the molecular basis for the disease primary hyperoxolauria type 1 (oxaluria) which is caused by a defect in an enzyme (alanine/glyoxlate aminotransferease) in the liver.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of the disease primary hyperoxalaria type 1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PH1 patients with the mitochondrial AGT phenotype have a more severe disease than expected for the levels of their AGT activity and that they may be candidates for liver transplantation.
the primary hyperoxalurias are caused by a deficiency in the activity and/or immunoreactive protein of AGT.
in the patients with the PH1, the AGT protein is either completely or partially missing, and that this protein is not peroxisome associated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PH1 patients with residual AGT activity are not a single group but can be subdivided into two groups, those with a peroxisomal defect and those with mitochondrial AGT.
the PH1 patients with residual AGT activity are not simply heterozygotes with one defective allele and one normal allele.

the PH1 phenotype is due to a combination of the severity of the AGT deficiency, which is determined by the specific mutations in the patient, and the location of the enzyme, which is determined primarily by the species and to some extent by the tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PH1 is a peroxisomal disease, but that it is possible for the disease to be caused by a trafficking defect that diverts peroxisomal proteins to other organelles.
PH1 is not a disease of peroxisomal deficiency, but a disease of mitochondrial deficiency.
it is important to look beyond enzyme activity and immunoblotting in the study of inborn errors of metabolism.
